If the hon. member wants to set up a meeting with Mr. Johnston of McGill University, I would be very pleased to accept, at his his invitation, any time.
Madam Speaker, I am glad of the opportunity of asking questions so that the Solicitor General will be able to acknowledge his presence here today.
Less than 10 per cent of the NDP is in the House.

Thank you for your intervention.
My question is addressed to the ever present Solicitor General. The Solicitor General and the House will be aware of the increased renewed public concern with the complete failure of the administration of justice to deal with the problems of sex offenders in our society arising out of the Timothy Garland case. While it is acknowledged that this case does not directly come within federal jurisdiction, it does give me the opportunity to raise with the minister the report on the management and treatment of sex offenders which his department and he made public on March 8.
Can the minister tell the House what steps, if any, he is taking to implement the recommendations of a report about which, frankly, all we have heard so far is deafening silence?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the concern of my colleague to underline my presence in the House. I am usually around, as he knows.
Perhaps some of the functions of the Solicitor General require a low profile, but I will try to enhance my presence or be more vocal in the House, so that even my own colleagues know that I am around.
With respect to the very important issue which my hon. friend raises, and it is an important issue, my hon. friend knows that on March 8, 1990,1 did release the report on the management and treatment of sex offenders. I indicated at that time that it would be part of the broader task force on mental health.

June 1, 1990
Routine Proceedings
I understand that all those recommendations are before my senior officials right now. I intend to look at those recommendations as soon as they are given to me.
I can assure this House, as I indicated on March 8, 1990, that that is not a report that will be accumulating dust on shelves.

Madam Speaker, while I appreciate the comments of the minister, there are a number of specific recommendations in that report which he could proceed with forthwith. The report makes it very clear that within Correctional Service Canada there are only 200 places in treatment programs for sex offenders and there are 1,400 sex offenders in our federal penitentiaries. Not only does the public safety require that immediate action begin in this area but so, too, the rights of sex offenders themselves. They desperately look for treatment when they are in our prisons.
Can the minister give us his personal assurance that he will proceed, right now, with some steps in this regard?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the report was released on March 8. There is a comprehensive task force with respect to mental health of which this report is a part. Some measures are already in place and others will continue to be put in place.
I would like to pick up on one comment I heard this morning in the debate on a specific piece of legislation. Someone complained that we should not be proceeding with piecemeal legislation. We are looking at a comprehensive review here and will be dealing with it globally.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General.
The Privacy Commissioner has stated that he did not censor the Legere and Gingras reports and that he had no problem with their release. The Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General has requested the production of the uncensored reports. There is a clear indication that there are major systemic and administrative problems at Corrections Canada and that a program
of weed and feed is necessary there. In light of all this, is the minister prepared to produce these reports immediately and to undertake an independent and comprehensive review of Corrections Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Solicitor General of Canada):

Madam Speaker, I have a number of petitions to present today relating to the tax benefit for northern Canadians.
The petitions state that, whereas the residents of northern Canada need a real tax benefit to recognize the high cost of living and working in areas described as northern or isolated, and whereas the report of the Task Force on Northern Benefits was released Friday, October 27, 1989, and it fails to address the needs of these communities, the undersigned call upon Parliament to reject the recommendations of the report and to develop a fair and equitable tax benefit program which recognizes the financial needs of the people in northern and isolated areas.
I would like to point out that residents of the following communities in my riding of Churchill have signed this
Routine Proceedings
petition: The Pas, Grand Rapids, Snow Lake, Moose Lake, Cross Lake, Cormorant, Sherridon and Thompson. There are also the signatures of people from Winnipeg and other communities including Terrace, B.C., and, from Newfoundland, Carmanville, Aspen Cove, Main Point, Ladle Cove, Deadman's Bay, Temple-man, Noggin Cove, Lumsden, Valleyfield, Musgrave Harbour, and also the community of Fredericton.
A number of communities obviously want the government finally to come up with a northern benefits package which benefits and helps the people who live in northern and isolated communities.

Madam Speaker, I have a petition certified as correct from the members and friends of the Ashby Branch 138 of the Royal Canadian Legion in Sydney.
There are almost 600 signatures on this petition and in part it states: "The government of Canada has introduced changes that will reduce homekeeping services to veterans and substantially increase the costs of longterm care. Whereas the veterans have already given service to this country and should not be targeted by those measures, the petitioners call upon Parliament to reject those budget measures which deprive veterans of proper services and increase their financial hardships.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs has made some movement away from this very Draconian position, but he has not gone nearly far enough. The position of the government is still grossly unfair to the veterans of the country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise to present a petition on behalf of numerous Canadians who are opposed to the goods and services tax.
Canadians by the hundreds have taken the trouble to sign this petition. They indicate their displeasure with the unfairness of the government in introducing this tax on virtually everything they purchase. They object to the fact that this is replacing the manufacturers' sales tax. They object to the fact that the government has already introduced 31 tax increases before the imposition of this particularly wicked and hard tax and they call upon Parliament to reject the goods and services tax.

June 1, 1990

speechtext: Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36,1 am tabling today a petition from Chibougamau in the riding of Roberval. Your petitioners reject the conclusions of the Task Force on Tax Benefits for Northern and Isolated Areas and ask that Chibougamau be recognized as an isolated area under the present tax benefit system.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present petitions pursuant to Standing Order 36. These petitions all urge the government to reject the GST.
It is interesting that when petitions are taken in Victoria, being the tourist destination that it is, petitioners come from all across the country, particularly from British Columbia. There is still, and continues to be, widespread public opposition to the GST and I have the honour to present these petitions to the House to that effect.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour of presenting a petition today that was organized by Mrs. Dorothy Macdonald of my riding, and signed by herself and many residents of the Ottawa area.
They petition Parliament to promote tolerance by acting to uphold the right to freedom of expression of the French-speaking minority in Ontario, and to uphold the right to freedom of expression of the English-speaking minority in Quebec.

Madam Speaker, once again I have the honour to present a petition with many signatures in both Chinese and English showing how strongly people from the Chinese Canadian community in British Columbia and merchants in Chinatown itself feel. It states: "The 7 per cent goods and services tax will hurt small businesses, costs will go up, incomes will go down and it will be an accounting
nightmare. The tax will also hurt consumers as prices of thousands of items and services go up."
"Therefore, the undersigned petitioners call upon Parliament and the Government of Canada to withdraw the goods and services tax." I only wish I could say it in Chinese as well.

Madam Speaker, I have a couple of petitions here today asking the government to reconsider its position with regard to the goods and services tax.
One petition in particular emphasizes the negative effects this tax will have on young athletes in sports organizations, something very vital to young Canadians. They are asking the government to take the unfair, unnecessary tax and reconsider its passage.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present two petitions today.
One is from seniors in the Trenton area of my riding who object to the government's policy of clawing back old age pensions. They ask the government to reconsider its policy with regard to this and reinstate old age security at its full value.

Madam Speaker, as well, I have the honour to present a petition from people across the country who are concerned about the goods and services tax to be introduced in January, 1991.
The petitioners find it an unfair and additional tax which makes the burden of taxation in the country absolutely impossible. They ask the government to reconsider and withdraw the legislation.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour and privilege to present two petitions pursuant to Standing Order 36.
The first petition is signed by over 200 people from different parts of Alberta, as well as from people in the Hamilton area of Ontario. It calls on the government to end low-level flying in Canada. These people object to low-level flights disrupting the hunting and traditional ways of the Inuit and other native people in Canada.

They are happy that the low-level flight training centre at Goose Bay has been cancelled. Nevertheless, flights are still escalating, and these people would like to see an end to it.

The
second petition I have is signed by people in my constituency from La Ronge, Stanley Mission, lie a la Crosse and other northern communities.
Like 80 per cent of Canadians, these people object to the imposition of the goods and services tax. They point out that it has a particularly negative impact on northerners who have already a much higher cost of living and pay much more for their goods and services.
Therefore, the petitioners call on Parliament, and in this case I presume members of the Liberal caucus who sit in the other place and have the power to do so, to bring an end to the goods and services tax.

Madam Speaker, I thank you and members of the House for agreeing to revert to Introduction of Private Members' Bills.
I rise today to introduce my private members' bill that would commemorate December 6 as a national day of mourning in memory of the 14 young women who were massacred in Montreal.
I envision this day of mourning also to be a day of action. Every day of the year, small committed groups of women carry the entire load for helping survivors of violence and educating the public.
I want to see the public at large become involved in working to stop violence against women, and I believe that this day of mourning could be a focal point for that kind of action.
I really do believe that this bill can obtain all party support and I certainly do hope that that is the case.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.
